Yes, couldn't agree more.

Step 1 is to identify the repeating mental patterns which cause us to make bad decisions.

Step 2 is to then implement rules or working practices which give us a fighting chance of not making the same mistake again.

Step 3 is to not get mad at yourself if you fail, simply to calmly realise your mistake, and reset to try again.

A "favourite" of mine - I am bored waiting for price to reach a level I want to trade, so I start scalping silly midrange PA on M1 in times of low volatility (M1 PA is much tougher to read when the market is slow). I then lose 0.5%. Annoyed, I try to make it back quickly. I lose another 1%. Then I get more annoyed, and double down on my next scalp. Then I lose 4%. Before I know it, I'm 15% in the red, and trebling my lot size on stupid scalps trying to just "win it all back in one go". All started from one silly boredom scalp.

When we stare at charts for many hours, it is easy to zone out. These are the times of real danger, because your conscious mind is not fully focused on what you are doing, and you can quite easily end up doing strange things that you wouldn't normally have dreamed of doing. I'm learning to spot when my mind has started drifting, and this is my cue to take a break and refocus.

Also, if you have entered a trade based on a setup, and find yourself wanting to close it long before it gets to the target, there are 2 options - write down on a piece of paper the reasons why you entered and why you think you should hold it to TG, and every time you find yourself wanting to exit too soon, just read what you've written. The second option, and the one I prefer, is to take partial profit, and just walk away from the desk and come back hours later. Many of my best trades are overnight POs which have had 8 hours to move in my favour without me messing with them

یک «علاقهٔ شخصی» من — از صبرکردن برای رسیدن قیمت به سطحی که می‌خواهم معامله کنم حوصله‌ام سر می‌رود، پس در زمان‌های نوسان پایین شروع می‌کنم به اسکالپ PA میان‌رنجِ احمقانه روی M1 (خواندن PA در M1 وقتی بازار کند است خیلی سخت‌تر است). بعد 0.5% می‌بازم. کلافه می‌شوم، سعی می‌کنم زود پس بگیرم. 1% دیگر می‌بازم. بعد کلافه‌تر می‌شوم و روی اسکالپ بعدی دوبرابر می‌زنم. بعد 4% می‌بازم. پیش از آنکه بفهمم، 15% در قرمز هستم و سایز لاتم را روی اسکالپ‌های احمقانه سه‌برابر می‌کنم تا فقط «همه‌اش را یک‌جا پس بگیرم». همه از یک اسکالپ از سر بی‌حوصلگی احمقانه شروع شد.

وقتی ساعت‌ها به چارت‌ها خیره می‌شویم، فکر از کار رفتن آسان است. این زمان‌های خطر واقعی هستند، چون ذهن هوشیارت کاملاً روی کاری که می‌کنی متمرکز نیست و می‌توانی به‌راحتی کارهای عجیبی بکنی که عادی هرگز رویایش را هم نمی‌دیدی. دارم یاد می‌گیرم بفهمم کی ذهنم شروع به سرگردانی کرده و این اشارهٔ من برای استراحت و تمرکز مجدد است.

همچنین، اگر معامله‌ای را بر اساس یک ستاپ وارد شده باشی و خودت را ببینی که خیلی قبل از رسیدن به تارگت می‌خواهی ببندیش، 2 گزینه هست — روی کاغذی دلایل ورودت و اینکه چرا فکر می‌کنی باید تا TG هولد کنی را بنویس، و هر بار که خودت را دیدی می‌خواهی زودتر خارج شوی فقط چیزی را که نوشتی بخوان. گزینهٔ دوم، و آن‌طور که ترجیح می‌دهم، برداشتن سود جزئی و رفتن از پشت میز و برگشتن ساعت‌ها بعد است. خیلی از بهترین معامله‌هایم PO‌های شبانه هستند که 8 ساعت فرصت داشته‌اند بدون دخالت من به نفعم حرکت کنند

Ah dudu, a typically constructive post delivered in your usual eloquent manner.

If anyone needs a translation I believe what dudu is trying to say is "I am surprised you are not having consistent returns. I tried RTM for a while, but could not find consistency with the method, so I returned to a simpler method of trading."

Well, it's a valid point. I've seen a lot of people come and go just over the last year on here, initially excited by the prospect of making 0 pip entries, and then leaving in frustration some time later, usually cursing IF. Let me say a few things in response.

First, the freely available material on RTM is NOT going to teach you how to make 0 pip entries. That would be madness to give away for nothing. What is does teach you are the concepts which you need to know, and apply over and over again, in order to develop your own understanding to the point where you can make 0 pip trades. Believe me, I've done it myself a large number of times by now. As IF has said, he has also given enough hints without spelling it out directly. I put together what he has said on here, and especially over at the FF thread, and figured out how he does it, and have been able to replicate it to a lesser extent. He's still much better at it than me though

Second, the reason I am not consistent has nothing to do with RTM, it's entirely my own fault. For me, trading is 25% skill, 75% mental control. I'm overconfident and impatient by nature and I hate to lose - I think it's not too hard to see why this is an awful combination for trading. Every time I sit down, I'm not only analysing charts, I'm also trying to fight my base personality. I hit far too many unconfirmed entries at dodgy levels, I boredom scalp, I use too much risk, I revenge trade.

But you see the difference between dudu and I, is that when I am failing to find consistency with a method that others are employing successfully, instead of cursing the system and the mentor who gave us the concepts. I assume ownership of my failure, and admit that the reason I'm not succeeding is due to my own failings. This is something we call intellectual honesty

Of course, the other option is to protect your ego, and tell yourself some pretty lie that the reason you didn't succeed with a proven method is not because you personally failed to apply it properly, but because the teacher is "BS".

Don't forget people - trading is HARD. There is pretty much zero chance you're going to pick this up and run with consistent profits in less than 12 months, at an absolute minimum. Sure, you can gain the analysis skills in much less time than that, but learning to control your own mental state and fight those elements of your brain that are constantly striving to sabotage you - well, that's the real battle, and that's what takes years of endless repetition. You also need this amount of time to really develop that "feel" for price, which cannot be quantified.

I've added 1000% to my account over a 12 day period. I've added 100% to my account even in a single day. But then I've gone on a madness revenge spiral and given it all back, or blown my account with a single stupid trade with no SL, which I kept adding to all the way.

As soon as I can stop self-sabotaging, my consistent returns and large sums of money are waiting for me. The only variable in the equation I still need to solve is me

اول، مواد رایگان موجود در RTM قرار نیست به تو یاد بدهد چطور ورودهای 0 پیپی بسازی. این را بی‌مجانی دادن دیوانگی است. چیزی که می‌آموزد مفاهیمی است که باید بدانی و بارها و بارها به‌کار ببری تا درک خودت را به نقطه‌ای برسانی که بتوانی معامله‌های 0 پیپی کنی. باور کن، خودم تا الان بارها این کار را کرده‌ام. همان‌طور که IF گفته، او هم سرنخ‌های کافی داده بدون اینکه صریح بگوید. من چیزهایی را که این‌جا و مخصوصاً در ترد FF درباره‌اش گفته جمع کردم و فهمیدم چطور این کار را می‌کند و توانستم به‌صورت محدودتری تکرارش کنم. با این حال، او هنوز در این کار خیلی بهتر از من است

دوم، دلیل اینکه سازگار نیستم هیچ ربطی به RTM ندارد؛ کاملاً تقصیر خودم است. برای من، معامله 25% مهارت و 75% کنترل ذهنی است. ذاتاً بیش‌خودباور و بی‌صبر هستم و از باختن متنفرم — فکر نمی‌کنم سخت باشد ببینی چرا این ترکیب فاجعه‌ای برای معامله است. هر بار که می‌نشینم، نه‌تنها چارت‌ها را تحلیل می‌کنم، بلکه دارم با شخصیت پایه‌ام می‌جنگم. ورودهای تاییدنشدهٔ زیادی در سطوح مشکوک می‌زنم، اسکالپ از سر بی‌حوصلگی می‌گیرم، ریسک بیش از حد می‌کنم، معاملهٔ انتقام‌جویی می‌زنم.

اما تفاوتی که dudu و من داریم این است که وقتی در یافتن سازگاری با روشی که دیگران با موفقیت به‌کار می‌برند شکست می‌خورم، به‌جای نفرین‌کردن سیستم و مربی‌ای که مفاهیم را به ما داد، مالکیت شکست خودم را می‌پذیرم و اعتراف می‌کنم که دلیل موفق‌نشدنم به نقص‌های خودم برمی‌گردد. به این چیزی می‌گوییم صداقت فکری

البته، گزینهٔ دیگر محافظت از غرورت است و به خودت دروغ نسبتاً قشنگی بگویی که دلیل موفق‌نشدنت با یک روش اثبات‌شده این نیست که خودت شخصاً نتوانستی درست به‌کارش ببری، بلکه این است که معلم «BS» است.

فراموش نکن رفقا — معامله سخت است. تقریباً شانس صفر است که این را برداری و در کمتر از 12 ماه با سودهای سازگار اجرا کنی، در حداقلِ مطلق. بله، می‌توانی مهارت‌های تحلیل را در زمان خیلی کمتری از این به دست بیاوری، اما یادگیری کنترل وضعیت ذهنی خودت و جنگیدن با آن عناصری از مغزت که پی‌درپی سعی می‌کنند خرابت کنند — خب، این نبرد واقعی است و همان چیزی است که سال‌ها تکرار بی‌پایان می‌طلبد. همچنین به این مقدار زمان نیاز داری تا واقعاً آن «حس» قیمت را بسازی که قابل‌کمی‌سازی نیست.

When we stare at charts for many hours, it is easy to zone out. These are the times of real danger, because your conscious mind is not fully focused on what you are doing, and you can quite easily end up doing strange things that you wouldn't normally have dreamed of doing. I'm learning to spot when my mind has started drifting, and this is my cue to take a break and refocus.

Also, if you have entered a trade based on a setup, and find yourself wanting to close it long before it gets to the target, there are 2 options - write down on a piece of paper the reasons why you entered and why you think you should hold it to TG, and every time you find yourself wanting to exit too soon, just read what you've written. The second option, and the one I prefer, is to take partial profit, and just walk away from the desk and come back hours later. Art wrote: Partial close is such a huge help. Have been doing it for quite some time now and works like charm with putting one at ease.

I just wanted to add that this too is saving my backside. I am also impatient and take trades on silly M1 cycles. And in my hubris, I think I have touch traded the bottom or top of an H4 swing and then next thing I know I am stopped out, watching a +5R or more trade turn into a -1R.

So, what I do is take 50% profit at 1R or the closest logical bounce point. That covers my risk completely. If I do get stopped out, it is very close to breakeven. Then if I do catch a nice swing move, I can let price take me out at a higher time frame Flag or FTR. And note: I do NOT change my Stop Loss. I leave it in place and simply take enough profits to cover any loss if I do get stopped out later.

I realize that this seems like a 'crutch' but it is my coping mechanism at the moment and it gives me peace to know that while I may not be fully mature at reading price, I can still make trades and learn successful money management skills at the same time.

geejay wrote: I realize that this seems like a 'crutch' but it is my coping mechanism at the moment and it gives me peace to know that while I may not be fully mature at reading price, I can still make trades and learn successful money management skills at the same time.

Not in the slightest, there's no point in ever allowing a trade that was in decent profit turn into an overall loss.

We can't possible ever *know* what the markets are going to do next, just be able to make a highly informed guess with good probability of success. We may think the planets have lined up in our favour, only to realise we've been mislead by a FO, or that what we thought was an engulf was a flip from some ignored level or SR etc.

It's just good sense to take some profit when it's on the table - whether that's in the form of taking most of the trade off at FTA or doing what you prefer and taking only enough profit to cover the SL, setting yourself up for a big payday if the setup works out.

And for sure, it's never a bad idea to leave your SL where you originally placed it, since price can so easily return to our entry levels hours or even days after we initially entered (in the case of higher scale setups), only to then later make it to our target.

posts.t:
The "solution", to call it such, would be to understand the move in terms of the higher scales, and also to study the move away from the FO level.

Let's say we are coming north strongly out of a W1 FTR, showing a engulf north on the D1 chart, price then "engulfs" south but shoots away from the zone like a rocket - then by combining all pieces of information available to us, we can be pretty certain that it was a FO, not an engulf.

Conversely, if there was a W1 eng south in play, price had RT'd up to some D1 bearish FTR, not broken it, and had then come down and "engulfed" the level - then we can be more certain in this case that it was an engulf, and not a FO.

Each piece of information the market gives us must be understood in context of the larger scale moves that are going on, and also considering how price approaches the level, and how it moves away.

Well, it's there on the chart really.

A bearish FTR has to engulf a bullish level south, make a RT north, and then *make lower lows*.

If price comes up north, RTs south, but then *does not make lower lows* and then goes on to *make higher highs*, then it cannot be a bearish FTR by definition. The swing high point is therefore *a place where a RT south started*, as opposed to *the edge of a bearish FTR*.

As discussed previously, individual instruments do not exist in a vacuum. The Fx market is driven by money flowing from one set of currencies into others. It is no coincidence that when an entire currency is about to make a turn, it's major and minors are usually all at significant levels at the same time. In this way we can also usually get a good guess at which directions large news announcements are going to go - 5-10 mins out from GBP news for example, go check the big picture on all GBP crosses, see if they are sat at important levels, or have just turned from important levels 30 mins ago etc.

If you're looking at a setup on an individual minor crosspair, and none of the other crosses for this currency are reflecting the same PA or are at good levels, then you should probably wait.

I've developed a style which is working well for me - I wait until highest probability levels only, based on higher timeframes and bigger picture analysis, then hit the market with very high risk (10-15%) sized over M10 ATR. This gives me the wiggle room to still get out of the trade with a profit even if my entry level breaks - provided I've waited until MPL to enter. If you jump in before MPL, and the level breaks, you have a far lower chance of getting out.

I usually just run the trade to LTF FTA, looking for 1R, or whatever I can get. I have a daily profit TG of 15%, and I can usually hit it in 1 or 2 trades.

I have closed out 30 of my last 32 trades in profit using this method - it works.

The downside? Well, because I just tend to close out my open trades as soon as I've reached my profit TG for the day, and I'm only entering at best levels, I am leaving a LOT of pips on the table. It is mind bendingly difficult to remain calm when you've got so much risk on the table, and very difficult to not just take your profit when you've hit TG.

This is a deliberate strategy however - 15% daily for 66 days compounds £100 into £1,000,000. In all actuality, I need a second account where I take the same entries, but with much lower risk, and run them properly. A different account for a different strategy, I don't believe it does any good to muddle different approaches into the same account.

posts.t:
MPL = max pain limit. It basically means the very last possible place price can turn from at the edge of a FTR, the last set of orders.

What you'll note is that very often, when an important level is broken, price makes an immediate quick RT back inside. Therefore if you wait only til MPL to enter, with a wider stop, you have every chance to escape what would been a loss with a profit instead.

posts.t:
My trading method is focused on the highest probability events only.

A price reaction from just inside MPL of an important FTR, or an engulf of MPL and then quick RT, are very high probability events. It allows me to profit 90% of the time. If price turns some distance away from MPL (although there is usually a good LTF reason for it to do so), then I just let it go without me. No problem, it won't be long to wait for the next chance.

If you were to look for shorts immediately when a level breaks like this, then you are essentially breakout trading, which is a high risk approach. Quite often price can make a deep RT after the engulf of a significant level. Safest is to wait for deepest possible RT level, and then enter short.

That was just some random PA from UJ M5 months ago. You can find examples of this phenomenon everywhere on any instrument. Just look for how price behaves when it reaches important levels - see how many times you get a valid reaction from FTB, and how many times it engulfs and then starts a RT.

Price can also smash straight through the level and not come back, but this generally means you read the HTF picture totally wrong, or were trying to enter from a non-important level.

قیمت می‌تواند هم مستقیم از سطح رد شود و برنگردد، اما این عموماً یعنی تصویر HTF را کاملاً غلط خوانده‌ای یا می‌خواستی از سطحی غیرمهم وارد شوی.
